content.title: How Dawn Staley built a winning basketball team and the fans to match
content.text: Nov. 11, 2016Updated March 30, 2017, 2:30 p.m. ETNearly 150 fans applauded the University of South Carolina women's basketball team as it entered Southside High for an open practice on a Thursday in mid-October.Head coach Dawn Staley waved to the spectators in the stands. A few players looked at the crowd and smiled. A couple of others danced to the music playing throughout the gym.Junior forward A'ja Wilson had a basketball in her hands less than a minute later, getting shots up before the team got to work.Before practice began, fans picked up team posters from tables in the school's common area and excitedly chatted with each other.Upstate resident Carolina Shiffer had never seen the Gamecocks in person until that night, and took advantage of the location being a short drive from her job.Shiffer was willing to speak with The Greenville News about her excitement ahead of the 2016-17 season, but made sure her seat in the gym was saved and her team poster was neatly secured before the interview took place.She didn’t want to miss the team’s entrance into the gym.“I can’t wait to see them all season, too,” Shiffer said. “We’re going to be champions, they’re going to be champions. I can’t wait to see it.”The bleachers eventually filled as people wrapped up work or finished with errands or school. Following practice, Staley introduced the team and answered questions like “Who’s your pick to win the WNBA championship?” and “Were you really on an episode of Martin?”It was a weeknight, and the gymnasium floor was filled with team supporters ranging from toddlers to teens to lifelong Gamecocks taking selfies, getting posters signed and meeting the USC women's basketball team.“It’s awesome to have people in the stands waiting for us to get here and it’s women’s basketball,” Staley said ahead of practice. “The state of South Carolina and the support it has given women’s basketball. It is like no other.”This is the culture Dawn Stanley created.Gamecock fans are proud of their SEC championships, the No. 1 national ranking in attendance and muse about the possibility of finally beating UConn this season.Eight years ago, conversations didn’t broach those topics. Staley had just arrived in Columbia after eight years as Temple’s head coach, and was officially announced on May 10, 2008.Staley, a three-time Olympic gold medalist and member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, held an 172-80 overall record at Temple, but chose to come to USC for a few reasons. She had family in the area. She had a chance to coach in the SEC. She appreciated the athletic department's commitment to the women's basketball program.In her first season, the team finished 2-12 in the SEC, placed 11th in the conference and ranked No. 45 in attendance nationally.But by 2011-12, the team made it to the Sweet 16.In April 2014, Staley landed the No. 1 recruit in the nation in Hopkins native A’ja Wilson, and by April 2015 the Gamecocks made a trip to the Final Four.South Carolina has led the nation in attendance for the last two seasons, first during 2014-15, averaging 12,293 fans in Colonial Life Arena for a total of 196,684 on the season.And while the numbers are great, the on-the-court wins aren't necessarily the deciding factor motivating fans to "buy-in" to the program.Mary Pink, Iowa State Associate Athletic Director for Marketing said when it’s time to make sports-related purchases, a personal connection to the team is key.At Iowa State, crowds show up for women's basketball – the Cyclones ranked No. 3 in attendance for 2015-16 and No. 4 the year before, which, for both seasons, is ahead UConn and Notre Dame.Pink gives a "bulk" of the credit for Iowa State's solid crowds to longtime head coach Bill Fennelly.Fennelly makes community outreach and interactions with fans a priority, according to Pink, and for at least the last 21 years, if Fennelly is asked to do an appearance or speak, he goes. He also places emphasis on thanking the fans."It's really having that one-on-one engagement with the fans, and I think that's very crucial for women's basketball, and for other sports," Pink said. "It really is, do you know the players, do you have a personal connection with the coach? Do you feel like you know him? For us that's been huge. And I think once, obviously Bill is winning, it drove them to want to go support, and go to the games."It was Staley who convinced Shiffer, a lifelong Gamecocks football, baseball and men's basketball fan, to add the women's basketball team to this list of USC programs she supports.“I love how she treats the fans,” Shiffer said. “We feel like a family. She treats the fans like we’re so important, and that is a fantastic thing.”Staley’s ability to win games while recruiting, connecting with fans and convincing tens of thousands of people to watch her team play has drawn comparisons to Tennessee's late, legendary head coach Pat Summitt.Those comparisons come from a journalist who has covered the Lady Vols since 1998.Maria Cornelius, longtime sportswriter and author of the “Final Season: The Preserverance of Pat Summitt,” says building a successful program is a formula that’s simple in ideology – promote the game – but tough in execution.If you follow Staley on Twitter, you’ll notice her updates are frequent and transparent. There’s no shortage of selfies, jokes and videos, but she also answers fans questions and provides what can feel like inside access into the program: pictures of team meetings, "you heard it here first" announcements and the infamous teasers.She’s engaging with fans. She’s replying and retweeting, making outsiders feel involved.Many coaches can’t – or couldn’t – manage, on top of day-to-day duties, having to market yourself and your team all the time.Summitt went to high schools and Kiwanis Club and opened practice for fans in Thompson-Boling Arena. Summitt built the Tennessee women's basketball program and brand, Cornelius said, and didn't stop promoting it after the team reached national success and recognition."Anywhere she could go to promote the Lady Vols, she went," Cornelius said. "And I see Dawn taking the same kind of approach.“It’s interesting to watch because I’m like, this is like watching what Pat did. You have to be willing to work pretty much, every day of the year. Dawn has been one of the coaches in women’s basketball that is willing to do that. The results show.”First-year Vanderbilt head coach Stephanie White also notices Staley's ability to communicate with fans honestly and keep them engaged, and mentioned that she loves it.“Her energy and her spirit and her ability to connect is critical," White notes, "That's one of the reasons that they've done what they've done from a fanbase standpoint."White and Staley were teammates on the Charlotte Sting during the 1999 season. White says being a part of the WNBA – a 20-year-old league, which was in its third season when they played together – gives both coaches a unique perspective of finding creative ways to promote their teams and keeping fans involved.The Gamecock women's basketball team recently participated in the popular #mannequinchallenge. Staley caught a touchdown pass at a South Carolina's spring football game and even brings her team around the state of South Carolina.Last year, the team took a trip to Charleston, and this year it was Greenville, ahead of the 2017 SEC tournament that will be hosted in Bon Secours Wellness Arena.After a Sweet 16 upset to end last season, USC started the year with No. 3 preseason ranking and a 92-80 win over No. 6 Ohio State on the road in its season opener.The matchup in Columbus, Ohio was not among the Gamecocks' 19 nationally televised games this season, but is a part of their tough non-conference slate featuring contests against UConn, Texas, Duke, Minnesota and UCLA.The program has given fans the opportunity to travel to the Duke, Auburn and Georgia road games with other fans through program-sponsored bus trips.But it's the matchup in Storrs, Connecticut with the defending-champion Huskies that's among the most talked about with fans."Definitely UConn is the one I’m most excited for," Shiffer said. "Because we’re going to beat them this year."There's also been an extension of the G-Hive, the program's $75 membership that includes five theme-based t-shirts for fans to wear on designated game days to match the team. Members have already been able to attend an open practice on Nov. 2 and Staley has tweeted about "exclusives surprises" to come.Immediately after Staley finished answering fan questions following the open practice in October, she hugged the first fan to approach her and ruffled an excited kid’s hair before shaking the hand of a man who reminded her of how they'd previously met.Then, she approved photo requests, including one from a mom whose toddler she'd held in her arms for the picture, before heading to a hallway outside of the gym to conduct another interview with the local news.In 2008, Staley said her vision is to bring "national prominence to the University of South Carolina."She did that, while igniting and nurturing a fanbase that will more than likely stick around for the long haul.“Dawn is really the blueprint, I think, collegiately," White said. "There’s no question that she’s got the blueprint that we all need to try to follow.”
